Judgment

1. Vide this judgment, I propose to dispose of the present appeal filed by the appellants against the impugned order dated 06.03.2020, whereby the Ld. Adjudicating Officer/Additional District Magistrate (Shahdara), Delhi imposed a penalty of Rs.60,000/ u/s 51 of the Food Safety &
Standards Act, 2006 (in short 'the FSS Act') upon each appellant.

sentences.text:
The facts in brief are that on 03.05.2018, Sh. Pankaj Kumar Meena, Food Safety Officer took a sample of 'Butter' for analysis from the FBO/Appellant No. 1 at Plot No. 6, Parmesh ComplexII,
Community Centre, Karkardooma, Delhi110 092.
The food article was stored there for use in preparation of Shahi Paneer, Butter Roti, Butter Naan etc., intended for human consumption.
The FSO tried to associate some public witnesses by requesting customers and passersby but none came forward.
Thereafter, the FSO requested Mohd. Zubair, FSO to join the proceedings as witness, to which he agreed.

At about 04:00 PM, the FSO purchased a sample of 'Butter' for analysis from the FBO/Appellant No. 1 and a credit note dated 03.05.2018 was prepared on the spot for payment of sample price but the sample price was not accepted because the article was not for direct sale.
The sample i.e. about 800 gm 'Butter', which was ready for use, was taken from an open container bearing no label declaration.

The sample of 'Butter' was taken after proper mixing of butter with the help of a clean and dry big spoon in a clean and dry steel container by rotating the same spoon in all possible directions several times.

Thereafter, the sample of food article was divided into four equal counterparts and put in four clean and dry glass bottles, and thereafter 16 drops of formalin was added in each counterpart of the sample with the help of clean and dry dropper.
Each bottle containing the sample was separately sealed as per the provisions of the FSS Act, 2006.
Notice in Form VA was prepared at the spot and copy of the same was given to the FBO/Appellant No. 1.
On 04.05.2018, one counterpart of the aforesaid sample of 'Butter' was sent to the Food Analyst.
The other two counterparts were deposited with the Designated Officer Dr. Pramod M. Kothekar.
As the FBO did not request to send the fourth counterpart of the sample for analysis to NABL accredited laboratory, it was deposited with the Designated Officer Dr. Pramod M. Kothekar.

3. The Food Analyst vide his report No. FSS/572/2018 dated 16.05.2018 opined that the sample is substandard because milk fat is less that the prescribed minimum limit of 80.0% and milk solids not fat exceeds the prescribed maximum limit of 1.5%.
4.
The FBO was given an opportunity to file an appeal against the report of Food Analyst.

The FBO preferred an appeal and one sample counterpart was sent to the Referral Food Laboratory,
Ghaziabad (UP).

The Referral Food Laboratory, Ghaziabad (UP) vide report No. 199/18/Jan/19 ND dated 17.01.2019 opined that the sample of 'Butter' does not confirm to the standards laid down in table below Regulation No. 2.1.10:1 of the Food Safety Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additive) Regulations, 2011, as the sample shows milk solids not fat above the maximum prescribed limit.

entities.text: Food Safety Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additive) Regulations, 2011
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The sample is thus substandard u/s 3(1)(zx) of the FSS Act, 2006.
5. Considering all the facts and circumstances of the case, the Ld. AO/ADM imposed penalty of Rs.60,000/ upon each appellant u/s 51 of the FSS Act, 2006.

6. Sh. Kundan Lal, Ld. Chief PP for the respondent has submitted that the Ld. AO/ADM has rightly imposed the penalties upon the appellants, as the sample of the food article was found to be substandard.

7. Per contra, Sh. Sandeep Mishra, Ld. Counsel for the appellants has submitted that the Ld.
AO/ADM has passed the order mechanically.
It has been submitted that appellants purchased the Butter from Amul and therefore, the appellants cannot be held liable.

It has been submitted that in Sh. Raj Nath Bhat vs Food Safety Officer on 11 February, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/85753783/

sentences.text: any case, Ld. AO/ADM has imposed very heavy penalty.
It has been submitted that atleast the penalty may be reduced as the appellants are poor persons and already having no income in the Covid period.
8. I have heard the submissions and perused the record carefully.
9. The Food Analyst as well as Referral Food Laboratory, Ghaziabad (UP) have opined that the sample of food article is substandard.

In State of Kerala Vs. Parameswaram Pillai Vasudevan Nair,
1975 Cri LJ 97, it was interalia held as under:
"14.The Act is a piece of consumer legislation.

entities.text:
State of Kerala Vs. Parameswaram Pillai Vasudevan Nair,
1975 Cri LJ 97
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It regulates to some extent the consumersupplier relations.
Consumerists demand enforcement of discipline among the producers or manufacturers of food to ensure safety in the realm of food.
The consumer's legitimate ignorance and his almost total dependence on the fairness and competence of those who supply his daily needs have made him a ready target for exploitation.
The Act is intended to protect him against outright frauds.
15. The Act does not make a distinction between cases coming under it on the basis of the degree of adulteration.
It does not provide for aggravation of offence based on the extent of contamination.
The offence and punishment are the same whether the adulteration is great or small.

Food pollution, even if it be only to the slightest extent,
if continued in practice, would adversely affect the health of every man, woman and child in the country.

Hence even marginal or border line variations of the prescribed standards under the Act are matters of serious concern for all and as public interests are involved in them, the maxim, de minimis non curat lex law does not concern itself about trifles, does not apply to them.
16. The standard fixed under the Act is one that is certain.
If it is varied to any extent the certainty of a general standard would be replaced by the vagaries of a fluctuating standard.
The disadvantages of the resulting unpredictability, uncertainty and impossibility of arriving at fair and consistent decisions, are great.
17. The Act does not provide for exemption of marginal or border line variations of the standard from the operation of the Act.
In such circumstances to condone such variations on the ground that they are negligible is virtually to alter the standard itself fixed under the Act.
18. The standards of qualities of the articles have been fixed by the Government under the provisions of the Act after due deliberation and after consulting a committee of competent men.
It is for them to give due allowance for probable errors before fixing a standard.
They may have done it also.
There is no reason to assume otherwise.
Therefore the conclusion is that for an article of food when a standard has been fixed under the Act it has to be observed in every detail."

sentences.text: Hon'ble Supreme Court in Raj Kumar Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh (2019) 9 SCC 427, interalia held as under: "7.We are of the considered view that once standards are laid down by the legislature then those standards have to be followed.

entities.text: Raj Kumar Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh (2019) 9 SCC 427
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In items like milk which is a primary food,
under the Act, it is not necessary to also prove that the food item had become unfit for human consumption or injurious to health.
In cases of food coming under the Act, it is not required to prove that article of food was injurious to health.
In this case, the only question to be determined is whether the article complies with the standards laid down or not?
If it fails to comply with the standards then it will have to be treated as an adulterated article even if it is not rendered injurious to health.
Even marginal deviation from the prescribed standard cannot be ignored."
The bare perusal of the above said law makes it clear that the provision such legislations have to be interpreted strictly.
It is also relevant to mention here that The Food Safety and Standards Act,2006 has already been diluted to a great extent.

entities.text: Food Safety and Standards Act,2006 has
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The punishment provided herein has been reduced to a large extent as compared to the earlier Food Adulteration Act.
In the interest of the society, it is necessary that the standards of foods have to be maintained strictly for the benefit of the society at large.
I consider that the plea of Ld. Counsel for the appellants that there was a slight variation and the Ld.AO/ADM should have given a benefit to the appellants, cannot be accepted.

11. In view of the above judgments, I consider that there is no need to interfere in the order of Ld.
AO/ADM.

However, in view of the facts and circumstances of the case and also the fact of unexpected Covid19 pandemic, the penalty imposed upon the appellants is modified to the extent that each appellant shall pay fine of Rs.20,000/.
Accordingly, the appeal is disposed of.
12. Record of Ld. AO/ADM along with copy of the judgment be sent back, and thereafter appeal file be consigned to Record Room.
13. Copy of the judgment be given Dasti to Ld. Counsel for the appellants.
